Issued at 500 PM CDT Mon Aug 17 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS:

- Certainly no truly "major" changes of note versus previous
  7-day "forecast package). As hopefully made clear in the Key
  Messages above, the varied thunderstorm chances these next ~
  60 hours (through Wed evening) without a doubt carry above-
  average uncertainty...not just regarding likelihood/areal
  coverage, but also severe potential (cannot really fault SPC
  for assigning Slight Risk to our entire CWA for Tuesday, but
  taking consensus of latest higher-res models (CAMs) at face
  value...it arguably could warrant more of a Marginal
  designation. 

- Big picture overview of the upper air pattern through the next
  7 days: Latest ECMWF/GFS agree that we will reside under
  either west-northwesterly or more "true" northwesterly
  flow...as we continue being positioned along the broad
  interface between dominant upper level ridging/high pressure
  off to our south or southwest...and broad low
  pressure/troughing off to our north or northeast. Given that
  we'll reside within this interface, we'll be prone to
  continued/intermittent rain/thunderstorm chances, and
  experience temperatures that are fairly typical/normal for
  mid-late August...with no noteworthy heat or coolness. 


-- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL DETAILS (through Mon. Aug. 24)
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SITUATION AS OF 4 PM:
Other than high temps ending up a few degrees warmer than our
initial early-AM forecast (most of our CWA on track to top out
85-90), today is turning out very much as expected. Under sunny
to mostly sunny skies, breezes are predominantly southerly and
not overly-strong...sustained speeds mainly 6-13 MPH with
occasional stronger gusts (especially north and west). 

In the mid-upper levels, water vapor satellite imagery and short
term model data confirm that we reside under west-northwesterly
flow, with the next low-amplitude shortwave disturbance
migrating out of WY into western NE. 


- THIS EVENING-OVERNIGHT:
Let the rain/thunderstorm chances and severe storm potential
uncertainties begin! Leaning heavily on latest HRRR runs (this
model performed quite well when this forecaster was on shift
last week) along with 12Z RRFS, our entire CWA likely remains
storm-free until at least 7-8 PM. Then, between then and roughly
midnight, mainly isolated/spotty storms could work into mainly
the northwestern 1/3rd of our CWA out of western NE (counties
mainly north and/or west of the Tri Cities). Should storms get
in, severe is certainly possible, with miexed-layer CAPE
(instability) of at least 1500-2500 J/kg and sufficient deep-
layer shear of 35-40KT suggestive of supercells with hail 
potential to around ping pong ball size/wind gusts to around 60 
MPH. 

Turning to beyond 12-1 AM, while any earlier activity south of
I-80 should mostly fade away, attention turns to especially our
northern/northeast counties (mainly north of I-80), as those
counties are most favored to PERHAPS be clipped by the
southern/southwestern fringes of a small convective cluster (or
two) that should MAINLY track just off to our north-through-
northeast. However, should any of this activity affect our area,
at least marginally severe hail/wind is again possible. 

In other departments overnight, low temps aimed mid 60s most
areas (more so upper 60s in KS), with fairly light-but-steady
southerly to southeasterly breezes persisting UNLESS an outflow
boundary surges through and abruptly turns winds
northerly/easterly. 


- TUESDAY DAYTIME (through around 7 PM):
Overall high-confidence in the "big picture"...as aloft a series
of disturbances will track overhead...while at the surface a
cold front will gradually pass through from north-to-
south...turning winds more north-northeasterly in its wake. 

Unfortunately, confidence in the "finer details" is admittedly
fairly low. Right off the bat in the morning, the first question
is whether a potentially strong (maybe even marginally-severe?)
cluster of storms is might be tracking south-southeastward
through mainly our northeastern/eastern counties? If this
occurs, it should exit our CWA off to the southeast by mid-
morning, with plenty of question marks whether any additional
strong/severe activity is able to form during the afternoon.
Again, latest higher-res models (namely HRRR/RRFS, but with
support from 18Z NAM) show very little afternoon activity within
our CWA...possibly due to residual weak capping as we reside 
"in between" disturbances. 

Otherwise, high temps were changed little, as we call for a
halfway decent gradient ranging from low 80s far north- 
northeast, to mid 80s central...to low-mid 90s mainly in KS (and
even upper 90s in especially southern Rooks/Osborne). In fact, 
parts of our far southern KS counties (Rooks/Osborne/Mitchell) 
could see heat index climb to at least 100-102 degrees (but 
should hold slightly short of Advisory criteria). 


- TUESDAY EVENING-OVERNIGHT (mainly after 7 PM):
